newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: MORE TALKS NEEDED WITH BONN ON WWII TREATY -HAVEL.
newsitem.headline: MORE TALKS NEEDED WITH BONN ON WWII TREATY -HAVEL.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel indicated on Thursday that further negotiations were still required with Germany on a long-awaited declaration aimed at closing the book on World War Two.

But one Czech official said he hoped that the declaration to be made by both countries' parliaments, which has become mired in German internal politics, could be issued in the second half of November.

Havel summoned Czech political leaders on Thursday to discuss the way forward with the declaration which belatedly tries to seal a reconciliation by covering both atrocities of the 1938-45 Nazi occupation and the post-war expulsion of the former Czechoslovakia's Sudeten German minority.

"They (the participants) expressed their views on the way further negotiations should be led," Havel said after meeting Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec, opposition chief Milos Zeman and other party leaders.
Havel told reporters that the text of the declaration should first be accepted by the two governments and then proposed to each country's parliament.
He gave no further details of what remained to be negotiated and whether it concerned the wording or the procedure for issuing the historic document.

One Czech diplomat said he hoped it could be signed after elections to the Czech Senate, which are scheduled for November 15 and 16 with a second round a week later. "The declaration is nearly ready and we expect it may be signed after the Senate elections," he said, requesting anonymity.

The Czech Republic is the only remaining victim of Nazi occupation not to have come to terms with Germany. Negotiations on the declaration have dragged on for more than a year, bedevilled by political pressures particularly in Germany.
Earlier hopes of completing it before lower house elections in May were dashed but there is consensus between the leading Czech parties on finishing the process as soon as possible.
Prague officials have repeatedly knocked the ball into the German court, where the declaration has become a hot potato.
Survivors of the 2.5 million Sudetens, who were expelled for supporting the Nazi occupation, and their descendents are a powerful lobby in the German state of Bavaria.

Through the Bavarian-based Christian Social Union, a member of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, they have exerted an influence on Bonn which Prague believes is out of all proportion to their numbers.

Havel has apologised for holding all Sudetens collectively guilty because a minority remained loyal to the democratic Czechoslovak state. But he has ruled out returning confiscated property to Sudetens, some of which has become valuable since the 1989 fall of communism.
